title: Bench criteria and risk screen
text:
Columns Rules Acceptance is binary Risk levels   Bench criteria and risk screen

  Release:   v18
  Use:   30 bench protocols in the tracker.

 BENCH-CRITERIA.csv  is a pre-run screen, not a legal risk assessment. Institutional biosafety, chemical-safety and waste rules supersede it. A protocol is   not ready   until the local supervisor signs the risk screen.

   Columns

-   risk level   — low, medium or high, based on biological, chemical, pressure, aerosol and data risk.
-   hazards   — what can hurt a person, a sample or the dataset.
-   controls   — engineering and administrative controls required before starting.
-   acceptance criteria   — what must be true to call the run valid.
-   failure triage   — first checks when the run fails.
-   data record   — the minimum metadata to save.

   Rules

1. No bench run without a named operator, date, protocol version and supervisor.
2. No result without a negative and a positive control where one exists.
3. No accepted run without the acceptance criteria met or a written deviation.
4. No sample without chain-of-custody and storage location.
5. No analysis without the raw data and the processing script.
6. Any contamination, injury, spill or near-miss stops the run and triggers the local incident process.

   Acceptance is binary

A run is   valid  ,   valid with deviation  , or   invalid  . “Looks fine” is not a result. Record the deviation and the reason.

   Risk levels

-   Low   — standard wet-lab or pure data work; normal PPE and local rules.
-   Medium   — aerosol, pressure, viable organisms, toxic solvent, or a decision that can waste a long experiment.
-   High   — any protocol that the local biosafety committee classifies as high; do not run without explicit approval. This module does not assign high risk on its own.

title: Mastery gates and calibration
text:
Weekly loop Gate criteria If a gate is failed Calibration review Portfolio reviews What this does not yet prove   Mastery gates and calibration

  Release:   v17
  Rule:   advance on evidence, not on calendar time.

   Weekly loop

1. Read the week's outcome in  OUTCOMES.csv .
2. Do the exit ticket closed-book. Score 0–3:
   - 3 = accurate, complete, transferable.
   - 2 = correct core, one gap.
   - 1 = partial or recognition-only.
   - 0 = cannot attempt.
3. Record confidence 1–5 in  CALIBRATION-TEMPLATE.csv .
4. If score <2, reread the specific section, redo the exit ticket, and retest after 24 hours.
5. If confidence − score ≥2, log the error and retest after 7 days.

   Gate criteria

| Gate | Week | Paper | Total | Section floor | Exit tickets | Portfolio |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| G1 | 7 | Paper 1 | ≥70% | ≥60% each | ≥80% at ≥2 | Repository scaffold |
| G2 | 18 | Paper 2 | ≥70% | ≥60% each | ≥80% at ≥2 | Reviews 1 artifacts |
| G3 | 26 | Paper 3 | ≥70% | ≥60% each | ≥80% at ≥2 | Strain design |
| G4 | 31 | Paper 4 | ≥70% | ≥60% each | ≥80% at ≥2 | 13C and MCA |
| G5 | 39 | Paper 5 | ≥70% | ≥60% each | ≥80% at ≥2 | Toolbox artifacts |
| G6 | 55 | Paper 6 | ≥70% | ≥60% each | ≥80% at ≥2 | Capstone dossier |

These thresholds are   course design decisions  , not an external standard. An external examiner must ratify them before the module claims validation.

   If a gate is failed

-   Total below 70%:   do not advance. Revisit the weakest section, redo the relevant exit tickets, and retake an equivalent paper after 7 days.
-   One section below 60%:   targeted remediation in that section only; retake that section or an equivalent.
-   Exit tickets below 80%:   repeat the weak weeks before the paper.
-   Portfolio below 3:   revise the artifact and re-review; do not substitute prose for evidence.
-   Two consecutive failures:   reduce load, review the error log with a supervisor, and rebuild the prerequisite week before another attempt.

See  EXAM-BLUEPRINTS.csv  for the per-paper remediation map.

At each gate, compute:

- mean confidence;
- mean exit score;
- calibration gap  confidence − score ;
- percentage of errors that were overconfident.

title: Pilot analysis
Pilot plan
text:
Slice Participants Measures Stop rules Analysis What the pilot cannot prove   Pilot plan

  Release:   v24
  Date:   7 November 2026
  Status:   designed, not run.
  Goal:   test whether 3–5 learners can use the module, reach the week-1–2 outcomes, and calibrate confidence.

   Slice

A four-week pilot is enough to test the loop without asking for 55 weeks:

- Week 1: cell as reactor.
- Week 2: water, pH and weak-acid toxicity.
- One brief: Brief 1  enzyme dossier  or the week-1 repository scaffold.
- One exit ticket per week, scored 0–3.
- One 20-minute usability interview.

   Participants

3–5 learners with a chemical engineering or biotechnology background. No personal health data. Use a participant code, not a name.

   Measures

| Measure | Target |
|---|---|
| Completion of two weeks | ≥80% |
| Exit-ticket score | ≥2/3 median |
| Calibration gap  confidence − score  | ≤1.0 |
| Broken-link or navigation failure | 0 |
| System Usability Scale | ≥75 |
| Claim-source check: find the source for one case-study number | ≥80% |

   Stop rules

- Any participant cannot find the tracker or lecture index → fix navigation before continuing.
- Any exit ticket scored 0 by two participants → rewrite the outcome or the explanation.
- Any claim-source check fails → fix the citation before more content.
- Distress or overload → stop, debrief, do not collect more data.

   Analysis

Use  PILOT-FORM.csv . Compute median exit score, mean confidence, calibration gap, completion and SUS. Report n, not percentages alone. Do not generalize from five people.

   What the pilot cannot prove

It cannot validate the full 55-week sequence, the exam thresholds, or long-term retention. It can only catch navigation, comprehension and calibration failures early.

title: Rubric guide
text:
Four dimensions Level definitions Scoring rules What “non-negotiable” means Portfolio review cadence Calibration   Rubric guide

  Release:   v17
  Use:   briefs, portfolio items and capstones.

   Four dimensions

Score every artifact on four dimensions, each 1–4.

1.   Evidence and provenance   — the claim is tied to data, a source, a page, an accession or a reproducible run.
2.   Method and calculation   — the method is appropriate, the arithmetic is checkable, units and assumptions are explicit.
3.   Interpretation and uncertainty   — alternatives are considered; intervals, limitations and falsification tests are stated.
4.   Communication and reproducibility   — a stranger can follow or rerun it; figures and tables are readable; limitations are not buried.

   Level definitions

| Level | Descriptor |
|---|---|
|   4 — Exemplary   | All four dimensions are explicit and traceable. The work survives an attempt to falsify it. A stranger can reproduce it from the stated files. |
|   3 — Pass   | All required deliverables are present. One dimension is thin but acknowledged. No unsupported central claim. |
|   2 — Revise   | A required deliverable is missing, a calculation is uncheckable, or a central claim is asserted without evidence. |
|   1 — Fail   | No primary evidence, the non-negotiable is absent, or the conclusion exceeds the data. |

   Scoring rules

-   Lowest dimension decides the overall score.   A 4 in communication does not rescue a 1 in evidence.
- A failed   non-negotiable   caps the overall score at 2, even if the writing is excellent.
-   Score 4 requires external review.   Score 3 requires course-reviewer sign-off.
- A portfolio item with no dated artifact scores 1, regardless of prose.
- A brief that recycles a published answer without the required primary data scores 1 on evidence.

   What “non-negotiable” means

Each brief has one. It is listed in  BRIEF-RUBRICS.csv . Examples:

- Brief 1: the bias of linearisation must be shown numerically.
- Brief 3: the balance must not be closed by scaling a measurement.
- Brief 8: the coupling must be proved from conservation, not asserted.
- Brief 14: the techno-economic verdict must be willing to be unwelcome.

Missing the non-negotiable is a 2 or lower.

- Review 2: week 31.

Use it throughout the course to practice moving from a process observation to a biological hypothesis, then asking what evidence would distinguish that hypothesis from alternatives. What the thesis reports Process: semi-continuous cassava retting in a moving-tray reactor, described as 60 kg/day, with eight trays and 2.5 kg of chips fed per tray each hour. The chips were 1–1.5 mm thick. The starter is named as Lactobacillus plantarum , Bacillus subtilis , and Aspergillus oryzae in most passages (8 L of each culture; 24 L total), but one starter-preparation passage says Aspergillus niger (printed p. 46 / PDF p. 70). No strain identifiers or independent identity check are given; treat the fungal identity as unresolved. The broth was circulated; the validation operated at an 8-hour tray residence time. Factors varied: residence time (8 or 12 hours), water-to-cassava loading, and broth-water replacement. The reported selected condition was 8 hours and a 7:1 water-to-substrate ratio. The replacement interval is inconsistent in the thesis: the abstract and methods say 25% at every residence time (8 hours), while the validation procedure says 25% every 4 hours; it was run for five days. Treat the interval as unresolved until the laboratory records are checked. Measurements: counts for L. plantarum and B. subtilis , gravimetric A. oryzae , broth pH, cyanogenic compounds in broth and flour, flour yield, moisture, swelling power, and whiteness. The reported validation averages include 35% flour yield, 13% moisture, 10.4% swelling power, and 83.5% whiteness. Keep the levels of explanation separate. The thesis reports process outcomes and microbial measurements. Its explanations—such as starch hydrolysis supplying glucose, L. plantarum acidifying the broth, or a consortium member limiting conversion—are hypotheses unless the corresponding substrate, metabolite, enzyme, or flux was directly measured. pH alone does not identify which acids were produced or quantify their rates. How to read this handbook This is the companion to the methods handbook, and it has the same relationship to machine learning that the methods handbook has to the bench: it is a set of written procedures and decision rules, not a tutorial, and none of it substitutes for having done the thing. Read it alongside Brief 16, which is the practical exercise, and week 30's identifiability work, which is the same problem in a mechanistic coat. Three framing points before any method. The field's data sets are small and that is the single most consequential fact. The authors of ART — the Automated Recommendation Tool, Radivojević, Costello, Workman and Garcia Martin, Nature Communications 11:4879 (2020) — state it plainly: data sets collected in synthetic biology are typically under 100 instances, which is not enough for deep learning, so their tool does not use it. A hundred constructs with four parts each is not a small version of a large problem; it is a different problem, where the variance of your performance estimate is often larger than the difference between the methods you are comparing. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 1 — The cell as a chemical plant — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 1 of 55 · Molecular foundations · Core The cell as a chemical plant Week content Case thread: Map the moving-tray reactor onto the cell. Which quantities are process variables, and which would be intracellular? Open the case thread . This week is a translation exercise, not a biology lesson. You already think in reactors, holdups, residence times and recycle loops; the cell is all of those at a scale where the numbers are unfamiliar. The aim is that by Friday you can state the size, composition and timescales of a cell from memory, say which compartment a pathway could live in and what that costs, and defend a host choice with numbers rather than with habit. Core ideas 1. The cell as a reactor, with numbers you should memorise An E. coli cell is roughly a cylinder 2 µm long and 0.8 µm across, so about 1 µm³ = 1 femtolitre. It is 70% water; the dry mass is around 3×10⁻¹³ g, of which 55% is protein, 20% RNA, 3% DNA, and the rest lipid, murein and small molecules. That gives about 2.5 million protein molecules and 10,000–70,000 ribosomes per cell depending on growth rate. Doubling time on glucose minimal medium is 40–60 minutes; on rich medium, 20. A yeast cell is 30–50 times larger by volume and divides in 90–140 minutes. The single most useful derived number: one molecule per E. coli cell is about 1.7 nM, because 1/(6.02×10²³ × 10⁻¹⁵ L) = 1.66×10⁻⁹ M. Carry that conversion; you will use it weekly. 2. Compartments are the engineering decision, not the biology trivia E. coli has cytoplasm and, because it is Gram-negative, a periplasm between inner and outer membranes. The periplasm is oxidising, so it is where disulfide-bonded proteins fold correctly, and it is a secretion destination industrially. Yeast adds mitochondrion (acetyl-CoA, TCA, iron-sulfur clusters, and its own genome), endoplasmic reticulum (membrane-bound cytochrome P450s and their reductase — the reason terpenoid and alkaloid routes go to yeast), peroxisome (beta-oxidation, and a useful isolated compartment for toxic intermediates), vacuole (storage and degradation), and the nucleus. title: Water, bonds and the chemistry of the cytosol
text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 2 — Water, bonds and the chemistry of the cytosol — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 2 of 55 · Molecular foundations · Core Water, bonds and the chemistry of the cytosol Week content Case thread: The thesis reports broth pH. What would distinguish lactate from other acids, and what remains unmeasured? Open the case thread . The chemistry of the solvent everything happens in. Engineers routinely skip this and then misread a pH-dependent titre collapse as a biological mystery. The week's payload is small and permanent: the four weak interactions and their energies, the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, and the mechanism by which a weak-acid product poisons the cell that makes it. Core ideas 1. The hydrophobic effect is entropic, and that is the whole point A non-polar solute in water forces the surrounding water molecules into a more ordered cage, which costs entropy. Aggregating non-polar surfaces together releases that ordered water, so the driving force for protein folding, membrane formation and substrate binding is largely the entropy of the released water rather than any attraction between the non-polar groups themselves. Consequences you will use: the hydrophobic core of a protein is not glued, it is squeezed; a bilayer assembles spontaneously; and a hydrophobic product will partition into the membrane rather than stay in the aqueous phase, which is the week 15 toxicity problem. 2. Four weak interactions, with their energies Hydrogen bond, 4–30 kJ/mol depending on geometry and environment. Ionic interaction, 2–20 kJ/mol in water (far stronger in a protein interior where the dielectric is low, which is why buried charges are rare and catalytically interesting when present). Van der Waals, about 1–4 kJ/mol per contact but numerous. Hydrophobic effect, context-dependent and entropy-driven. Compare these with a covalent bond at 350–450 kJ/mol and with thermal energy RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol at 310 K. Two conclusions: individually these interactions are barely above noise, so specificity comes from many of them acting together over a complementary surface; and a protein's folded state is only 20–60 kJ/mol more stable than its unfolded state, which is a handful of hydrogen bonds. 3.

text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 3 — Protein structure and folding — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 3 of 55 · Molecular foundations · Core Protein structure and folding Week content The catalyst is encoded, folded, degraded and evolvable — four properties your reactor catalysts never had. This week builds the structural vocabulary you need to read an enzyme's datasheet critically, and it plants the two facts that govern protein engineering in week 37: folding is marginally stable, and activity and stability trade against each other. Core ideas 1. Four levels, and which interactions hold each Primary is the covalent sequence, which determines everything else. Secondary is local backbone hydrogen bonding: α-helix with 3.6 residues per turn and i to i+4 bonding, β-sheet parallel or antiparallel with inter-strand bonding, and turns. Tertiary is the three-dimensional fold, held by the hydrophobic core, plus hydrogen bonds, ionic pairs and sometimes disulfides. Quaternary is subunit assembly, which matters to you because it determines whether a gene deletion removes the activity — a heteromeric complex is an AND in the gene-protein-reaction rule of week 21, and that distinction is a leading source of false essentiality predictions. 2. Transcription in bacteria, in the detail you will actually use RNA polymerase holoenzyme is core plus a sigma factor; the sigma determines promoter recognition, so swapping sigma factors switches whole regulons. A σ70 promoter has a −35 and a −10 hexamer with a spacer, and promoter strength is largely how well those elements match consensus — which is why promoter libraries are built by mutating them. Memorise RT = 2.577 kJ/mol at 310 K, so a ten-fold concentration ratio is worth 5.93 kJ/mol and a thousand-fold is worth 17.8. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 15 — Lipids, membranes, transport and uptake — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 15 of 55 · Quantitative physiology · Useful next Lipids, membranes, transport and uptake Week content Substrate must get in and product must get out. Uptake kinetics sets your maximum rate; export, or its absence, sets your toxicity ceiling. Most failed strain designs fail at the membrane rather than in the pathway, and this week is where you learn to spot that before building anything. Core ideas 1. The bilayer, and why a hydrophobic product is a membrane problem A phospholipid bilayer is about 4 nm thick with a hydrophobic interior equivalent to a thin oil phase, and its fluidity is tuned by fatty acid chain length and unsaturation — which is how cells adapt to temperature and to solvents. A hydrophobic product partitions into that interior according to its octanol-water coefficient, so the aqueous titre you measure is not the concentration the membrane experiences. As it accumulates the bilayer disorders, the proton-motive force leaks, membrane proteins lose activity, and the cell arrests. This is why alcohols above about C4, terpenoids and many aromatics have titre ceilings well below their stoichiometric ones, and why the countermeasures are efflux pumps, membrane engineering, or in situ product removal rather than more pathway flux. 2. Fatty acid synthesis: the acetyl-CoA and NADPH sink The cycle extends a growing chain by two carbons per round, using malonyl-CoA as the extender and consuming two NADPH per round. A C16 fatty acid therefore costs 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 ATP for the carboxylations and 14 NADPH. Two consequences. Lipid is the most expensive cell component per gram, which is why lipid content matters in a biomass equation. And malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, is held at very low concentration and tightly regulated — which is why flavonoid, polyketide and fatty-acid-derived products are so often precursor-limited at the first step, and why acetyl-CoA carboxylase overexpression appears in so many of those papers. 3. title: Growth kinetics and physiological states
text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Appendix — Fermi drills Appendix — on the numbers in these notes Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 18 — Growth kinetics and physiological states — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 18 of 55 · Quantitative physiology · Core Growth kinetics and physiological states Week content Case thread: Separate counts, growth rate and metabolic flux. Which did the thesis actually measure? Open the case thread . Growth is autocatalysis with a catalyst whose composition changes. Everything in phase 4 is parameterised by what you learn to measure this week, and the week's real lesson is about identifiability: which parameters a given experiment can determine, and which it cannot however good the fit looks. Paper 2 is sat at the end. Core ideas 1. The balances, and why they are the ones you already write Batch: dX/dt = µX and dS/dt = −µX/Y − mX, with µ a function of S. Chemostat with a sterile feed: dX/dt = (µ − D)X and dS/dt = D(S₀ − S) − µX/Y − mX. Setting the derivatives to zero gives the steady state, and the first consequence is the one that makes the chemostat valuable: µ = D. You set the growth rate by turning a pump. Washout follows when D exceeds the maximum µ attainable at S₀. All of this is a CSTR with a self-reproducing catalyst, and nothing in the mathematics is unfamiliar — the biology is in the form of µ(S) and in the maintenance term. 2. Monod, and its honest status µ = µmax S/(Ks + S) is empirical, not mechanistic: it has the Michaelis-Menten form because saturation is a general property of carrier-mediated uptake, but it describes whole-cell growth rather than one enzyme, and Ks is not a binding constant for anything. It fails in predictable ways — at very low substrate where maintenance dominates, under multiple limitation, during transients where the cell's composition lags, and for inhibitory substrates, where Haldane-type or other forms are used instead. Use it as a convenient interpolation and say so; treating Ks as a physical constant of the organism is a common and visible error. 3. title: Genome annotation and what it is worth
meta: Week 19 of 55 · Constraint-based modelling · Useful next
text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 19 — Genome annotation and what it is worth — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 19 of 55 · Constraint-based modelling · Useful next Genome annotation and what it is worth Week content A reconstruction is only as good as the annotation beneath it, and annotation is mostly inference rather than measurement. This week you learn how a genome becomes a gene list, how often that list is wrong, and how to judge the evidence behind any functional assignment you later rely on. It is the least glamorous week in the phase and it is what stops you trusting a model more than it deserves. Core ideas 1. How a genome becomes a gene list, and where inference enters Sequencing gives contigs; gene calling finds open reading frames by codon statistics and ribosome binding site context; then function is assigned, almost always by homology to something already annotated. That last step is where the uncertainty lives. A BLAST hit at 70% identity over most of the length is strong evidence of a shared fold and reasonable evidence of a shared reaction class; it is weak evidence of identical substrate specificity, and essentially no evidence about which cofactor the enzyme prefers. Orthologues, which arose by speciation, usually keep function; paralogues, which arose by duplication, frequently diverge — so annotation transferred along a paralogue is the single commonest source of a reaction in a model that the organism cannot actually perform. 2. Evidence codes, which you should read before any annotation Databases record how a function was assigned, and the classes differ enormously in strength: experimental characterisation in this organism; experimental in a related organism; inferred from sequence similarity; inferred from genomic context such as operon membership or gene neighbourhood; and automatic electronic annotation with no curator involvement. In a typical bacterial genome, somewhere between a tenth and a third of metabolic genes have experimental evidence in that organism and the rest are inferred. Validating against essentiality data and then explaining every disagreement is what separates a modeller from someone who has run a tutorial, and it is the single most valuable artifact you will produce in this phase. Core ideas 1. How essentiality is predicted, and the threshold hiding inside it Delete a gene by applying the GPR logic, constrain the affected reactions to zero, re-solve, and compare predicted growth with the wild type. Then apply a threshold: below some fraction of wild-type growth, typically 1% to 10%, the gene is called essential. That threshold is a modelling choice and it matters — a gene whose deletion leaves 5% growth is called essential at a 10% threshold and non-essential at 1%, and experimentally such a strain grows slowly rather than not at all. Report the threshold you used and show the sensitivity to it; many published screens do neither. 2. title: Metabolomics and intracellular measurement
meta: Week 27 of 55 · Measurement and control of flux · Core
text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 27 — Metabolomics and intracellular measurement — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 27 of 55 · Measurement and control of flux · Core Metabolomics and intracellular measurement Week content Case thread: What sampling would be needed to see intracellular pools rather than broth? Open the case thread . Every concentration you assumed in phase 2 and every bound you guessed in phase 4 is measured this week, badly and with difficulty. The content is not the instrument; it is the error budget, and the skill is knowing which term dominates and whether your conclusion survives it. Core ideas 1. Turnover time is the design constraint, and you compute it τ = pool / flux through the pool, and the whole protocol follows from it. Work in µmol gDW⁻¹: intracellular water is about 2 mL gDW⁻¹, so 1 mM is 2 µmol gDW⁻¹. ATP at 1.5 mM against a turnover flux of order 50 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ gives τ ≈ 0.2 s; glucose-6-phosphate at 1 mM with a glycolytic flux of 10 gives τ ≈ 0.7 s; glutamate at 60 mM drained at 1.5 gives τ ≈ 290 s. Three orders of magnitude separate the easy case from the hard one, which is why no single protocol serves a whole metabolome. Rank your metabolites by τ before choosing one. 2. Quench speed and leakage are in direct conflict Rapid arrest and membrane integrity trade against each other, because the fastest methods work by cold shock or solvent and both perturb the membrane. How much leaks depends on the organism, the metabolite class, the solvent, the temperature, the biomass density and the contact time, so the figures are protocol-specific and must be validated rather than assumed: reported losses for cold methanol run from a few per cent for nucleotides to half the pool for some organic acids. Fast filtration is gentler, slower, and the wash itself removes metabolite. The answer is the differential method: quench whole broth, measure the filtrate separately, and take the intracellular amount as the difference, n_in = n_broth − n_extracellular. That estimates the intracellular pool only when the two measurements are commensurate — matched volumes, accounted recovery, no filtration delay — and it converts an unknown bias into a variance rather than removing it. 3. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 29 — 13C metabolic flux analysis II: estimation, statistics and design — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 29 of 55 · Measurement and control of flux · Core 13C metabolic flux analysis II: estimation, statistics and design Week content Case thread: Which 13C tracer would resolve the split, and what precision is needed? Open the case thread . The inverse problem. Fitting fluxes to labelling data is nonlinear estimation with an unpleasant covariance structure, and the statistics is where most published MFA is weakest. Three things separate a flux claim from a flux opinion: a multi-start optimisation, an interval from a method that does not assume local linearity, and a goodness-of-fit test you are prepared to let fail. Core ideas 1. The objective, and why it is minimised a hundred times Weighted least squares: minimise Σᵢ ((xᵢ,meas − xᵢ,sim(v))/σᵢ)² over the free fluxes, with x_sim from week 28's forward model. The weights are not cosmetic — unweighted, a precise fragment and a noisy one speak equally, and the σᵢ are what turn the residual sum into a statistic with a known distribution. The surface is nonlinear with local minima, so one run is not a result. Restart from random points until the best objective has been recovered repeatedly — how many that takes depends on the dimension, the bounds, the parameterisation and the optimiser, so report the strategy and the spread of objective values you obtained rather than a round number. Restarts landing on several distinct minima of similar objective value signal a genuine identifiability problem rather than a numerical one. 2. Chi-squared is the model's check on itself At the optimum, and only if the weighted residual model is correctly specified, the objective is compared against a chi-squared distribution. Counting the degrees of freedom is where this goes wrong: it is the number of independent data constraints minus the rank of the fitted model, and MDV elements are not independent — each vector sums to one, so one element per fragment is fixed by the others, and natural abundance correction couples them further. title: Kinetic models of metabolism
meta: Week 30 of 55 · Measurement and control of flux · Useful next
text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 30 — Kinetic models of metabolism — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 30 of 55 · Measurement and control of flux · Useful next Kinetic models of metabolism Week content Where dynamics returns. A kinetic model answers questions no stoichiometric method can touch — concentrations, behaviour away from steady state, which enzyme controls the flux — at the price of parameters nobody can measure in vivo. The craft is in handling that price: thermodynamic consistency imposed as a constraint, parameters carried as ranges, and an ensemble reported instead of one fit with a false precision. Core ideas 1. What a kinetic model buys, and when it is the wrong tool Four things FBA cannot give: metabolite concentrations, time-dependent behaviour, the response to a change in enzyme level, and control coefficients. The cost is a rate law and several parameters per reaction, and the parameters are the problem — in vitro kcat and Kₘ come from dilute buffer at saturating substrate, while the cell is crowded, at a different pH, and working near Kₘ by design. The decision rule is scope: model the sub-pathway you have a specific dynamic question about, ten to twenty reactions anchored by measured concentrations, and use FBA for anything genome-scale. Whole-cell kinetic modelling is usually the wrong first move. 2. The reversible rate law and the Haldane relation For one substrate and one product, v = (V_f·S/K_S − V_r·P/K_P)/(1 + S/K_S + P/K_P). Four parameters, but not four free ones: at equilibrium v = 0, giving K_eq = (V_f·K_P)/(V_r·K_S). That is the Haldane relation, and since K_eq is fixed by ΔrG′° only three of the four may be fitted. Impose it as a constraint rather than checking afterwards. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 33 — Vectors, expression systems and chassis preparation — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 33 of 55 · The molecular toolbox · Useful next Vectors, expression systems and chassis preparation Week content Where the construct lives decides how it behaves, and the decisions are quantitative: an origin fixes copy number and so both dosage and segregational stability, a marker commits you to a recurring cost at production scale, a promoter choice sets an inducer bill per cubic metre. The arithmetic most often skipped is the one this week insists on — how many generations a seed train actually takes, and what fraction still carries the plasmid when it gets there. Core ideas 1. Copy number is a property of the origin's control circuit Initiation is negatively regulated by a plasmid-encoded antisense RNA or iteron, so copy number is set by a feedback loop and mutations in it move the set point. The usable grades are high (pUC-type, hundreds), medium (p15A and pBR322-type, tens), low (pSC101-type, a handful) and broad-host-range (pBBR1-type, modest and transferable across proteobacteria). Treat published numbers as ranges that depend on host, growth rate and temperature, and note that output saturates in dose: Shuler’s §14.5 rule of thumb is that 25 to 50 copies roughly doubles protein while 50 to 100 gives less than a doubling, because transcription, translation and folding capacity are shared. Two plasmids sharing a control circuit are incompatible, which is why multi-plasmid designs take origins from different families. 2. Segregational loss is set by the copy-number distribution, not the mean For random partition the probability of a plasmid-free daughter is P = 2^(1−Z) with Z the number of independent replicative units. Shuler's Example 14.1 makes the point: 40 single copies give P = 1.8 × 10⁻¹²; if half the DNA is dimers and a fifth tetramers the units fall to 12 + 10 + 2 = 24 and P = 1.2 × 10⁻⁷; and a population split half at 10 copies and half at 70 — the same mean of 40 — gives P = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴, some 5 × 10⁸ times worse. This week turns that into construction: how far each dial really moves expression, how large the resulting library is, whether the screen can cover it, and how to measure the cost of the extra protein without fooling yourself with the wrong control. Core ideas 1. The dials are unequal, and they multiply Between a gene and a working catalyst sit copy number (roughly 1–50× across usable origins), promoter strength (about three orders of magnitude across a characterised library), translation initiation set by the ribosome binding site and 5′ UTR structure (two to three orders), codon usage (a few fold), and folding and proteolysis (0–100% of what was translated). The ranges multiply, so promoter and ribosome binding site together already cover more range than any pathway needs: the problem is resolution within it, not reach. Resolution is where prediction runs out — initiation depends on Shine-Dalgarno spacing, 5′ UTR folding energy and the gene’s first codons, which fold into the same structure, so calculators rank variants usefully but predict absolute rate only to about an order of magnitude. They build a spread to measure rather than specify a level. 2. Architecture carries information the parts list does not In an operon, position matters: transcripts are degraded from the 5′ end and polymerase falls off, so downstream genes are expressed less and gene order is itself a dial. Insulating with a ribozyme or strong terminator removes the coupling, and terminators are graded rather than binary, so read-through into a downstream module is a common reason a part behaves differently in context. meta: Week 35 of 55 · The molecular toolbox · Useful next
text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 35 — Genome editing: recombineering, CRISPR and multiplexing — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 35 of 55 · The molecular toolbox · Useful next Genome editing: recombineering, CRISPR and multiplexing Week content Chromosomal engineering at scale. Every editing method persuades a repair pathway to do something useful, so knowing which repair biology each depends on predicts which will work in a host nobody has edited before — and predicts, correctly, that most published protocols do not transfer. The week ends in an editing plan, which means a biosafety section as much as guides. Core ideas 1. The repair pathway available decides the method A break is repaired by homologous recombination, which uses a donor and is precise, by non-homologous end joining, which is error-prone and needs none, or by microhomology-mediated end joining in between (Lee §10.1). Most bacteria have little or no end joining, so an unrepaired break is lethal — which is why Cas9 in a bacterium is a counter-selection against unedited cells rather than a mutagen, and why a donor must be supplied. Eukaryotes have the opposite problem: end joining dominates and competes with the donor, so knockouts come easily and precise edits do not; Lee §10.1 puts homologous integration in mammalian cells at about 1 in 1,000 transfected cells. 2. Recombineering makes a bacterium recombinogenic, and counter-selection makes the edit markerless Gam blocks the exonuclease that would destroy linear DNA, Exo resects one strand, Beta anneals it at the replication fork. Datsenko and Wanner (PNAS 97:6640, 2000) showed PCR products carrying only 36–50 nt of homology suffice, and that the cassette can then be removed by FLP acting on flanking FRT sites; oligonucleotide recombineering needs Beta alone and no selection, so its limit is detection. Without a nuclease the markerless route is two selected events: the cassette integrates under positive selection, then excises under a counter-selection — sacB on sucrose, rpsL in a streptomycin-resistant host, upp on 5-fluorouracil, manP on mannose, or an I-SceI site. This week is library arithmetic, and the arithmetic is unusually unforgiving: the number of transformants needed to see 95% of a saturation library rises so fast with the number of randomised positions that the design decision is made before any enzymology is considered. The content is how positions are grouped and which codon alphabet is used, because those two choices move the requirement by six orders of magnitude, and they are made from structure and consensus data rather than from intuition. Core ideas 1. Three strategies differ in what they require you to know, not in what they achieve Rational design needs a structure, a mechanism and a hypothesis about which residue does what; it tests a handful of variants and is cheap when the hypothesis is right and worthless when it is wrong. Directed evolution needs only a screen and makes no claim about mechanism, which is why it works on properties nobody can predict — expression, solubility, tolerance of a cosolvent — and why it costs library-sized effort. Semi-rational design uses structure to choose where to randomise and evolution to decide what to put there, which is the dominant mode in practice because structural information is now cheap and screening still is not. The governing fact is an asymmetry in the data: there are over 100 million protein sequences and over 100,000 structures, and almost no sequence-to-function measurements. Everything these models can and cannot do follows from that, and so does the only honest way to test them — which is not a random split. Core ideas 1. The data asymmetry is the whole explanation Protein Engineering Ch 6 states the position plainly: UniProt holds more than 100 million unique sequences and the Protein Data Bank more than 100,000 experimentally determined structures, both growing exponentially, while data mapping sequence to function remains scarce. The chapter's further observation matters more than the counts — function data is hard to standardise because it depends on assay conditions and even on who ran the assay, so statistical models are most useful on data generated by one group under one protocol. Two consequences follow. Models trained on sequences alone can only have learned what evolution constrained, because that is the only signal in the training set. Data is cheap and a model revision is not: the scarce skill is turning a measurement into a changed assumption rather than into a figure. Two ideas carry the week. A genome-scale model is a context for omic data rather than a consumer of it, which is what separates integration from curve-fitting; and the circularity risk is real — a model constrained by expression data and then validated against expression data has been told what to say. Networks as context for content, and the two kinds of network this contrasts Palsson Ch 24 opens on the distinction and Table 24.1 tabulates it. Inference-based networks are built from correlation and recurring pattern in the data itself: they need no prior knowledge, apply wherever there is data, relate directly to the omic measurement, and rewire substantially when more data arrives. Knowledge-based reconstructions are built from biochemistry: they are directly mechanistic, require that the biochemistry be known, obey mass and charge conservation and thermodynamics, relate more closely to phenotype through fluxes, and do not rewire once reconstructed. The consequence that matters is stated directly — statistical correlation between omic variables does not confer causality, whereas contextualising the same variables in a mechanistic network can establish it, because the network says which measurements are allowed to co-vary. 2. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 44 — Clostridia, actinomycetes, fungi and photosynthetic hosts — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 44 of 55 · Hosts, products and the literature · Useful next Clostridia, actinomycetes, fungi and photosynthetic hosts Week content The specialists, and the week where the matrix has to stop being a list of organisms and start being a comparison on one basis. Four host classes, each of which exists in industry because it does one thing no model host can: clostridia ferment gases and make four-carbon solvents anaerobically, actinomycetes carry the assembly-line enzymes that make most of the antibiotics in the pharmacopoeia, filamentous fungi secrete protein at concentrations nothing else approaches, and photosynthetic cells fix their own carbon. Each carries a correspondingly specific difficulty, and in three of the four cases the difficulty is a transport problem rather than a genetic one — gas into liquid, oxygen into a viscous broth, photons into a volume. The habit from weeks 40 to 44 — derive the ceiling, then read the published number as a fraction of it — is necessary here but no longer sufficient, because a bulk product can sit at 90% of theoretical and still lose money. Three further terms decide it: the substrate bill at the achieved yield, the utilities bill that aerobic operation adds, and the allowance left for recovery once the first two are paid. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 48 — Heterogeneous reaction, immobilisation and reactor choice — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 48 of 55 · Process, economics and the application · Useful next Heterogeneous reaction, immobilisation and reactor choice Week content The week where a chemical engineering degree needs no translation at all, and the one place in this course where the biology is the easy part. A catalyst you can retain is a catalyst you can starve, and the whole content is the arithmetic that decides how big the particle may be. Three texts give the same problem three different ways and it is worth seeing why: Doran's generalised Thiele modulus divides by three for a sphere, Plawsky's divides by three inside the square root, and Shuler's does not divide at all, so the same bead can have a modulus of 0.7, 0.7 or 2.1 depending on whose definition you picked up. The number that matters is not the modulus but the effectiveness factor, and the safe route — the one that works when you do not know the intrinsic kinetics, which is almost always — is Weisz's observable modulus, which is built from the rate you measured rather than the rate you assumed. Core ideas 1. Immobilisation is five chemistries and one trade, stated as what each costs Shuler §3.4.1 lists the methods and Doran §12.1 the reasons; put them in the order of what they do to activity. Adsorption is cheap, reversible and leaks — the enzyme comes off with ionic strength or shear, so the catalyst has a half-life rather than a lifetime. Covalent attachment does not leak but reacts with residues that may be in the active site, so activity retention is typically a fraction rather than all of it, and the fraction has to be measured per enzyme. Entrapment in a gel — alginate, carrageenan, polyacrylamide — retains activity well because the protein is never chemically touched, and introduces the diffusion problem that is the rest of this week; it also leaks anything smaller than the mesh, which for an enzyme means slow loss and for a whole cell means none. The chain is short — strain physiology gives an oxygen uptake rate, the uptake rate gives a required k_L a, the required k_L a gives a power input, the power input gives a heat load, and the heat load gives a cooling duty — and at production scale it does not close on air at atmospheric pressure. The honest part of this week is the uncertainty: Doran's own k_L a correlation states that it was derived in vessels up to 4.4 m³, agrees to within 20-40%, and overestimates transfer in vessels up to 25 m³ by about 100%, so a 50 m³ design is outside the correlation's range altogether. The right response is not a better correlation. It is to notice that the uncertainty in k_L a is larger than the difference between the design options, and to choose on the things that are certain — the oxygen balance, the heat balance, and Shuler's Table 10.2, which is arithmetic rather than correlation. The content is a selection problem — a train of unit operations chosen from the product's physical properties — and the thing that makes it a quantitative week rather than a catalogue is that stage yields multiply while stage costs add. Ten stages at 95% each give 59.9% overall, which is the arithmetic every proposal with a long purification train has not done. The second organising number is Shuler's: recovery and purification exceed 50% of manufacturing cost, especially for intracellular products, and the fraction rises as titre falls, from roughly half at a citric-acid titre to roughly nine-tenths at a therapeutic-protein titre. That is why titre and product location outrank yield in this week, and why the strain decisions that look like downstream decisions — secrete or not, excrete or not — are the expensive ones. Core ideas 1. The train is selected from four physical properties, not from a flowsheet Size, solubility, volatility and charge, in that order of coarseness, and each one maps to a family of operations. Size separates cells from broth and, at the other end of the scale, separates the product from everything bigger or smaller than it: filtration and centrifugation at the micron scale, micro- and ultrafiltration at the sub-micron, nanofiltration and reverse osmosis at the molecular. Solubility decides between extraction, precipitation and crystallisation. Volatility decides whether distillation is available, which for ethanol is the whole process and for a protein is never. Charge decides ion exchange and electrodialysis, and in combination with solubility it decides isoelectric precipitation. Open the case thread . The week where the previous fifty-one get audited. A techno-economic model is not a summary of the design; it is an independent calculation that the design has to survive, and the usual outcome of doing it properly for the first time is that something upstream turns out to be incoherent. That happens here: the anchor carries the 50 m³ vessel from week 49 and the 67.3% recovery train from week 51 through a proper factored capital estimate, and the cost of goods comes out at about $61 per kilogram against the $12 per kilogram the week 51 anchor assumed the product sells for. Nothing in the arithmetic is wrong. What is wrong is the pairing of a pilot-scale vessel with a commodity price, and no amount of strain engineering fixes it — the same calculation says the titre would have to reach about 300 g L⁻¹, or the plant would have to reach about 50,000 m³, which is within a factor of two of the fermentation volume in the NREL cellulosic ethanol design. The organising result of the week is the one that makes that diagnosis repeatable: the elasticity of cost to a parameter is the cost share of the lines that parameter moves . Titre moves every line that scales with annual output, which here is 96.8% of cost, so its elasticity is −0.97; yield moves only the raw-material line, 3.2% of cost, so its elasticity is −0.03. The ranking is not a property of biology. It is a property of where the money is, and it is computed, not argued. Core ideas 1. text: Week content Core ideas Worked anchor Reading map Common misconceptions Check yourself before moving on Apply it to your fermentation experience Teach it back Week 53 — Capstone I: the strain — Metabolic engineering ← Lecture index Auto Light Dark Week 53 of 55 · Process, economics and the application · Core Capstone I: the strain Week content No new reading and no new technique: the week's whole content is assembling fifty-two weeks of separate artifacts into one document that a stranger can check. That sounds like editing and it is not, because the act of putting the chain in one place is what exposes the joints — a stoichiometry that was balanced in week 17 against a biomass equation that changed in week 26, a thermodynamic feasibility established at 1 mM when the process runs at 300, a deletion set validated against a model whose medium is not the medium week 47 designed. The discipline that makes the week worth a card of its own is that every number in the dossier has to carry its provenance and its uncertainty, and the second of those is where most capstones fail: a predicted yield quoted to three significant figures from a flux balance is not a prediction, it is a bound on a bound. Core ideas 1. What the dossier is for, and the test it has to pass One reader, one hour, no author present. A supervisor reading this document is deciding two things — can this person formulate a question, and will they finish things — and both are answered by whether the numbers connect rather than by whether they are impressive. The practical test is that a stranger can take any number in the final performance estimate and walk it backwards to a measurement, a published value with a section pointer, or an explicit assumption, without asking the author anything.
